clinicalPearls: A benign proliferation of the lactiferous ducts within the nipple, presenting as erosion, crusting, ulceration or a palpable nipple nodule.
Frequently accompanied by serous or blood-stained discharge from the nipple surface.
Clinically and macroscopically mimics Paget's disease of the nipple, making biopsy essential for diagnosis.
Most commonly affects middle-aged women but can occur at any age and rarely in men.
Histology shows florid adenosis and papillomatosis of the nipple ducts with preserved myoepithelial layer, confirming its benign nature.
Management is complete surgical excision, which is curative and confirms the diagnosis.
Immunohistochemistry for myoepithelial markers helps distinguish it from tubular carcinoma and Paget's disease.
Because it can coexist with carcinoma, thorough sampling of the excised specimen is important.
reference.pathophysiology: Nipple adenoma is a benign tumour arising from the collecting ducts of the nipple, characterised by a compact proliferation of ductal epithelial and myoepithelial cells forming adenotic and papillary structures. The proliferating ductal tissue may erode the overlying epidermis, producing the surface ulceration and discharge that clinically resemble Paget's disease. Retention of a continuous myoepithelial cell layer around the proliferating tubules is the key feature confirming benignity and distinguishing the lesion from invasive carcinoma, although sclerosis and epithelial crowding can create a worrying pseudoinfiltrative appearance.
additionalDifferentials: Squamous cell carcinoma of the nipple
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination of the nipple-areola complex
Mammography as part of triple assessment
Punch or excisional biopsy of the nipple lesion
Histopathology with assessment of the myoepithelial layer
Immunohistochemistry for myoepithelial markers (p63, smooth muscle myosin)
redFlags: Failure of an eroded nipple lesion to heal, requiring biopsy to exclude Paget's disease
Associated deep breast mass or suspicious microcalcification
Histological loss of the myoepithelial layer suggesting malignancy
Coexisting invasive or in situ carcinoma in the specimen
reference.prognosis: Nipple adenoma is benign and complete excision is curative, with recurrence uncommon and generally attributable to incomplete removal. It carries no intrinsic malignant potential, although rare coexistent carcinoma should be excluded.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lesion for Paget's disease and vice versa without biopsy
Misinterpreting the pseudoinfiltrative pattern as tubular carcinoma on histology
Treating a persistent eroded nipple as eczema and delaying biopsy
Incomplete excision leading to local recurrence
Failing to sample the specimen adequately and missing coexistent malignancy

management: Perform complete surgical excision of the lesion, which is both curative and definitively diagnostic
Obtain biopsy before or at excision to confirm the diagnosis and distinguish it from Paget's disease of the nipple
Undertake triple assessment with clinical examination, retroareolar ultrasound and mammography to exclude a coexistent carcinoma
Confirm benignity on histopathology by demonstrating a preserved myoepithelial layer, supported by immunohistochemistry (p63, smooth muscle myosin)
Reassure the patient of the benign nature and lack of intrinsic malignant potential once carcinoma is excluded
Follow up to detect the uncommon recurrence, which usually reflects incomplete removal, and manage through a breast multidisciplinary service
